extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, corporate communicators, advertisers, and students of PR
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations counsel on planning and executing propaganda/PR campaigns: analyzing client and public, formulating policies, choosing channels and leaders, ethical constraints, and applying mass-psychology techniques to win public approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and use of molders of public opinion (group leaders)
rubrics_metrics.description: If we set out to make a list of the men and women who... might fairly be called the molders of public opinion... It would obviously include, the President... Senators and Representatives... presidents of the chambers of commerce... newspaper and magazine editors... authors... theatrical or cinema producers... leaders of fashion... influential clergymen... presidents of colleges and universities... financiers... amateurs of sport, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target the relatively small set of group leaders or 'invisible wirepullers' because influencing them influences the larger groups they sway; recognize that many visible leaders are themselves led by lesser-known influencers; examples in text show political bosses, fashion leaders, editors, clergy, university presidents, financiers, and producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of the public relations counsel (scope of role)
rubrics_metrics.description: The propagandist who specializes in interpreting enterprises and ideas to the public, and in interpreting the public to promulgators of new enterprises and ideas, has come to be known by the name of 'public relations counsel.' He functions primarily as an adviser to his client, very much as a lawyer does. A counsel on public relations concentrates on the public contacts of his client's business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover every phase of the client's ideas, products or activities that may affect the public or in which the public may have an interest; act as adviser on public contacts analogous to legal counsel on legal matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client analysis before any campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: His first efforts are, naturally, devoted to analyzing his client's problems and making sure that what he has to offer the public is something which the public accepts or can be brought to accept. It is futile to attempt to sell an idea or to prepare the ground for a product that is basically unsound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the product, the markets, the way the public reacts to the product, the attitude of employees to the public and towards the product, and the cooperation of distribution agencies; modify the client (e.g., orphan asylum reorganized on 'cottage plan', or recommend different product forms such as a safe girdle rather than the old corset) rather than attempt impossible persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience analysis and segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: He studies the groups which must be reached, and the leaders through whom he may approach these groups. Social groups, economic groups, geographical groups, age groups, doctrinal groups, language groups, cultural groups, all these represent the divisions through which, on behalf of his client, he may talk to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which groups must be reached and the particular leaders or institutions that influence them; use this segmentation to select tactics and intermediaries (e.g., physicians for food claims, school teachers for child-focused campaigns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulation of policies and client conduct before publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Only after this double analysis has been made and the results collated, has the time come for the next step, the formulation of policies governing the general practice, procedure and habits of the client in all those aspects in which he comes in contact with the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agree on policies governing client behavior and public-facing practices prior to publicity; PR must shape client actions (not just messages) to gain approval and acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of diverse media channels and coordination with advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: The means by which the public is apprised of the actions of his client are as varied as the means of communication themselves, such as conversation, letters, the stage, the motion picture, the radio, the lecture platform, the magazine, the daily newspaper. The counsel on public relations is not an advertising man but he advocates advertising where that is indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and coordinate among many channels—personal, print, broadcast, events—and work cooperatively (not duplicatively) with advertising agencies when appropriate to complement PR efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific study and monitoring of public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern propagandist studies systematically and objectively the material with which he is working in the spirit of the laboratory... he studies the field by means of a clipping service, or of a corps of scouts, or by personal study at a crucial spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic monitoring (clippings, scouts, field study) to determine trends, features losing appeal, and which actors influence purchase decisions; recognize that exact scientific accuracy is impossible and build in a margin of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage leaders and associative processes to create trends
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can influence the leaders, either with or without their conscious cooperation, you automatically influence the group which they sway... The modern propagandist therefore sets to work to create circumstances which will modify that custom... He appeals perhaps to the home instinct... organizing an exhibition... inviting key people (famous violinist, popular artist, society leader)... these key persons affect other groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange events, exhibitions, or uses by key influencers so their endorsement and behavior create associative prestige that spreads through professions and the public (e.g., architects copying masters; fashion leaders setting modes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create circumstances to remove sales resistance rather than direct attack
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of assaulting sales resistance by direct attack, he is interested in removing sales resistance. He creates circumstances which will swing emotional currents so as to make for purchaser demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indirect methods—exhibitions, staging, influential advocates, architectural integration, social proof—to make the public voluntarily request the product ('Please sell me a piano') rather than pressing it on them directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and manipulation of clichés and symbols in the group mind
rubrics_metrics.description: When the example of the leader is not at hand and the herd must think for itself, it does so by means of cliches, pat words or images ... By playing upon an old cliche, or manipulating a new one, the propagandist can sometimes swing a whole mass of group emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and use entrenched clichés or create new associative symbols to reframe perceptions (examples: tagging a candidate with 'interests', using 'Bolshevik' to frighten, renaming hospitals as 'evacuation posts' to reset expectations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand unconscious motives and symbolic desires
rubrics_metrics.description: It is chiefly the psychologists of the school of Freud who have pointed out that many of man's thoughts and actions are compensatory substitutes for desires which he has been obliged to suppress... A thing may be desired not for its intrinsic worth... but because he has unconsciously come to see in it a symbol of something else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek the true motives underlying behavior (status, exhibitionism, maternal impulses, snobbishness) and craft campaigns that appeal to these deeper symbolic desires rather than stated rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical code: client selection, candor, and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: The profession of public relations counsel is developing for itself an ethical code... he nevertheless refuses a client whom he believes to be dishonest, a product which he believes to be fraudulent, or a cause which he believes to be antisocial... He should be candid in his dealings. It must be repeated that his business is not to fool or hoodwink the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refuse clients with dishonesty, fraud, antisocial aims, or conflicts; do not accept hopeless or unmarketable cases; be candid, label propaganda material as to source so editors and the public know origin and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous vigilance and rumor control
rubrics_metrics.description: The counsel on public relations must maintain constant vigilance, because inadequate information, or false information from unknown sources, may have results of enormous importance... attempt to stop [rumors] at their source, counteracting them promptly with correct or more complete information through channels which will be most effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain ongoing information efforts as needed; monitor and promptly counteract rumors and false information; build relations of confidence so rumors cannot take root (e.g., protect stock value, public trust).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovering and developing new markets
rubrics_metrics.description: His function may include the discovery of new markets, the existence of which had been unsuspected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use public-relations surveys and initiatives (contests, exhibitions, community assistance) to reveal or create demand segments and new markets (examples: Ivory soap sculpture contests, railroads helping communities to foster right-of-way growth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of group-formation activities and institutional sponsorship
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most effective methods is the utilization of the group formation of modern society in order to spread ideas. An example of this is the nationwide competitions for sculpture in Ivory soap, open to school children... The contest was held under the auspices of the Art Center in New York City, an organization of high standing in the art world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design campaigns that mobilize schools, professional institutions, and competitions; secure respectable institutional sponsorship and distinguished judges to lend prestige and embed the product in social routines (school curricula, exhibitions, prizes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Find overlapping or disinterested interests to recruit leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: The leaders who lend their authority to any propaganda campaign will do so only if it can be made to touch their own interests. There must be a disinterested aspect of the propagandist's activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the campaign so that sponsoring or endorsing it aligns with leaders' genuine interests or public-minded causes (e.g., art educators sponsoring soap sculpture because it cultivates aesthetics), thus securing authentic authority and avoiding purely paid endorsements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act as broad adviser on public-facing aspects (analogous to lawyer)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawyer concentrates on the legal aspects of his client's business. A counsel on public relations concentrates on the public contacts of his client's business. Every phase of his client's ideas, products or activities which may affect the public or in which the public may have an interest is part of his function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a comprehensive advisory stance—recommend operational changes, customer-facing policies, employee conduct, product presentation and distribution—that together improve public perception and acceptance rather than only issuing messages.
